title: Assent: common to historic and living; specific justifying act beyond bare assent (Ames)
source_text: LXV. Quod spectat ad assensum, reperiuntur inter Reformatos unus & alter qui negant illum esse fidei actum, sed solum quid fidem praecedens, & ab ea praesuppositum. Caeteri vero communiter assensum inter actus fidei numerare solent. In eo tamen videtur esse aliquis dissensus inter Theologos Ecclesiae Romanae, & inter Scholae Reformatae Doctores, quod priores illi quidem praecipuum fidei actum consistere velint in assensu qui toti Verbo Dei adhibetur, id vero negant Reformati. Verum si quis propius inspiciat mentem Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, agnoscet illos, dum docent fidem in assensu proprie consistere, loqui de fide simpliciter & absolute considerata, & prout abstrahitur a fide tam viva quam mortua, minime vero agere de eo quod fidem vivam, quae sola actu justificat, a mortua distinguit. Reformatorum vero mens est assensum esse quid commune fidei mortuae, quam historicam vocant, & fidei vivae, quae sola salutem & justitiam affert: ac proinde proprium & specificum actum fidei, quatenus salvat & justificat, alia in re quam in nudo & simplici assensu statuendum & collocandum esse. Et ita quoad rei summam videntur utrique, hac etiam in parte inter se consentire. Amesius autem, & si qui alii sint qui negent assensum esse fidei salvificae actum, id solum sibi volunt, assensum non esse id quod fidem salvificam ab historica & mortua discernit.
pass_a_gloss: As for assent, there are found among the Reformed one or another who deny that it is an act of faith, but only something preceding faith and presupposed by it. The rest commonly are accustomed to number assent among the acts of faith. Yet in this there seems to be some dissent between the theologians of the Roman Church and the Doctors of the Reformed school, because the former want the principal act of faith to consist in the assent given to the whole Word of God, which the Reformed deny. But if anyone looks more closely into the mind of the Doctors of the Roman Church, he will recognize that when they teach that faith properly consists in assent, they speak of faith simply and absolutely considered, and as it is abstracted from living as well as dead faith, and by no means deal with what distinguishes living faith, which alone actually justifies, from dead. But the mind of the Reformed is that assent is something common to dead faith, which they call historic, and to living faith, which alone brings salvation and justice: and therefore the proper and specific act of faith insofar as it saves and justifies is to be established and placed in something other than bare and simple assent. And so as to the sum of the matter both sides seem to agree with each other even in this part. But Ames, and if there are any others who deny that assent is an act of saving faith, mean only this: that assent is not what discerns saving faith from historic and dead faith.
pass_b_english: A few Reformed deny assent is a faith-act; most number it among faith acts. Rome puts principal act in assent to the whole Word; Reformed deny that for living faith specifically.

Rome speaks of absolute faith; Reformed say assent is common to historic and living, so the specific saving act lies beyond bare assent — Ames means assent does not mark off saving from historic faith.

lemmas.latin: quid commune fidei mortuae ... & fidei vivae
lemmas.gloss: something common to dead faith and living faith

choices.why: Specific justifying act beyond shared assent.
rejected: assent alone suffices as living-faith differentia
